title: Getting 401 Unauthorized
body: Check your PANDASTACK_API_KEY is set and valid. Get a new token from dashboard settings.

title: Getting 429 Too Many Requests
body: You've hit the API rate limit. Back off and retry.

title: Getting 503 Service Unavailable - no agents
body: No agents available. Contact support if this persists.

title: Getting 507 Insufficient Storage
body: Agent disk full. Volume provisioning failed — contact support or delete unused volumes.

title: Sandbox not responding or stuck
body: Check sandbox logs. Try exec with shorter timeout or restart the sandbox.

title: Database connection refused
body: Ensure TLS is enabled. Check connection_url from GET /v1/databases/{id}.

title: Can't create sandbox - no capacity
body: The cluster has no free capacity. Delete unused sandboxes or add another agent host.

title: Using sandbox for machine learning / AI
body: Use code-interpreter template with Python. Install packages via exec or custom template.

title: Networking — NATID mode
body: PandaStack uses a network mode called NATID (NAT-identity-preserving) to deliver fast snapshot restores. Understanding it matters when you're debugging connectivity. The problem Firecracker snapshots include the kernel's network state — interface IPs, ARP tables, DHCP leases. If we restore a snapshot into a VM that has a different IP than the one baked into the snapshot, the guest networking is broken until DHCP renegotiates. title: Networking
body: Every sandbox lives in its own Linux network namespace with a tap device carrying the template's baked guest IP and MAC. That baked identity is a per-template constant, so two sandboxes of the same template genuinely have the same guest IP — the namespace is what stops them colliding. Each sandbox also gets a unique /30 on a veth pair, which is the address the host actually dials. Guests reaching each other is prevented by an explicit firewall rule , not by the namespacing. title: Scheduler
body: PandaStack has a tiny global scheduler — a handful of SQL queries plus a deterministic scoring function — that picks the right agent host for every create. It's not Kubernetes; it doesn't need to be. The whole thing fits in one file. The decision Whichever agent scores highest wins the create. title: Snapshot & Restore
body: PandaStack doesn't cold-boot Linux every time you ask for a sandbox. We boot Linux once at template-bake time, write the entire VM state (memory + CPU registers + device state) to disk, and on every subsequent create we that state into a fresh Firecracker process and let it execute the very next instruction.
